The Election of 1948. Harry Truman's shocking upset victory over heavily favored Thomas Dewey defied virtually every poll and political prediction of the era. Running against a do-nothing Republican Congress and a fractured Democratic Party split by southern segregationists and Henry Wallace's Progressive Party, Truman won forty-nine point six percent of the popular vote and three hundred three electoral votes.

Thomas Dewey, the heavily favored Republican governor, was so confident he took few campaign risks; polls showed him winning by double digits. Harry Truman, the incumbent Democrat, campaigned as a scrappy underdog, attacking the Republican do-nothing Congress with fiery rhetoric. Strom Thurmond's States' Rights Democrats captured the white South's segregationist vote; Henry Wallace's Progressive Party split the liberal left. The Democratic base seemed irretrievably fractured; Truman appeared finished.

Truman won the popular vote narrowly and the electoral college decisively, carrying key industrial states—Ohio, Illinois, Pennsylvania. His famous whistle-stop campaign tour—traveling by train and speaking from the rear car—energized working-class voters and attacked Dewey's elitism. The Chicago Tribune's premature Dewey Defeats Truman headline became an iconic symbol of prediction failure and democratic surprise.

The States' Rights defection proved temporary; southern Democrats returned by nineteen fifty-two but grew increasingly alienated by the party's civil rights stance. Truman's victory validated his foreign policy: aggressive containment of communism, support for Israel, and the Marshall Plan. The civil rights movement would be foreshadowed by the southern Democratic defection in this election.
